q: Which of these children does NOT need urgent evaluation?
o: Boy, 9, with sudden onset scrotal pain
Newborn with hydronephrosis in a solitary kidney
Boy with sickle cell disease and priapism
e: Asymptomatic microhaematuria is not an emergency; its commonest identified cause is hypercalciuria, though most is transient with no cause found. Bilateral hydronephrosis or hydronephrosis in a solitary kidney, acute scrotal pain (torsion until proven otherwise) and priapism in sickle cell disease need urgent care. Gross haematuria in a newborn is an emergency (renal vein or artery thrombosis).

q: Which statement about lower urinary tract reconstruction in children is FALSE?
o: CIC must be accepted before surgery
No test guarantees voiding after augmentation
Exstrophy patients make up most cases
e: Myelomeningocele (spinal dysraphism) makes up the vast majority. Lapides' clean intermittent catheterisation (1972) allowed aggressive correction of storage with a good outlet. CIC must be taught, practised and accepted preoperatively, because no test ensures spontaneous voiding afterwards; the urethra should be checked for easy catheterisation.

q: A 10-year-old has left flank pain and microscopic haematuria. The first imaging test is:
e: Ultrasound is the imaging of choice for suspected stones or known stone formers, avoiding radiation. Paediatric stone disease is rising sharply, especially in adolescent girls.

q: Which mycobacterium is NOT in the M. tuberculosis complex?
e: M. bovis, M. africanum and M. microti cause TB; BCG derives from M. bovis and can cause disease. M. avium-intracellulare is a nontuberculous mycobacterium.

q: Which statement about primary (endemic) bladder stones is FALSE?
o: They form without a predisposing cause
They are commoner in girls than boys
They peak at 2 to 4 years of age
They are linked to poor nutrition
e: Primary bladder stones form without obstruction, infection or foreign body; they occur in undernourished children (low animal protein, low urine output, altered pH), most under 10 years, peak 2–4 years, much commoner in boys. Children present with abdominal discomfort, dysuria, frequency and haematuria; pulling at the penis is considered pathognomonic.

q: Which statement about the female pelvis is FALSE?
o: Pelvic floor tone helps passive continence
The levator ani attaches to the ATFP
The female inlet is heart shaped
e: The female inlet is oval and wider (male heart-shaped), contributing to pelvic floor weakness. The inlet faces anteriorly so abdominal pressure is directed onto bone, not muscle and fascia. Resting tone of pubococcygeus, puborectalis and iliococcygeus supports viscera and maintains passive continence. ATFP (arcus tendineus fascia pelvis) and ATLA (arcus tendineus levator ani) are distinct; ATFP is the main fascial attachment; levator ani attaches to it and covers obturator internus.

q: Which statement about candidacy for orthotopic neobladder is FALSE?
o: A healthy urethra and sphincter are essential
Older age and obesity are contraindications
e: Diversion evolved from conduits to continent cutaneous to orthotopic. Neobladders allow volitional voiding without an appliance; CISC needed in a minority. 80–90% of men and 75% of women are candidates; a healthy urethra and sphincter are required. Age and obesity are not contraindications (older men regain continence more slowly but most achieve it; a neobladder may suit an older man living alone). Continent diversion needs eGFR >35–40 mL/min and ability to concentrate and acidify urine. Possible after pelvic radiation or radical prostatectomy in selected patients.

q: After radical prostatectomy, biochemical recurrence (AUA/EAU) is defined as PSA:
e: AUA 2007 (Cookson): ≥0.2 ng/mL confirmed by a second value >0.2; higher thresholds are more specific but less sensitive. (Nadir + 2 ng/mL is the post-radiotherapy Phoenix definition.) A transient PSA rise needs close monitoring: not all men progress to biochemical, let alone clinical, failure.

q: Which is NOT a reason the child's kidney is vulnerable to trauma?
e: Children have little visceral (perirenal) fat, a less protective chest wall, relatively larger and more mobile kidneys. Blunt renal trauma is managed nonoperatively except major vascular avulsion or extensive extravasation.

q: Which statement about bladder storage pressure in children is FALSE?
o: Drugs plus CIC lower filling pressure
e: Compliance arises from unfolding, elasticity and viscoelasticity (stress relaxation balances filling). Chronic passive filling pressure >40 cmH2O impairs ureteral drainage, causing acquired VUR, hydronephrosis and falling GFR. Anticholinergics plus CIC lower filling pressure, especially with detrusor overactivity. Cystometry: room-temperature or body-temperature saline or contrast at 10% of expected capacity per minute (CO2 is unreliable). Expected capacity (book): 30 × (age + 2) mL, or 7 × weight (kg) in infants (ICCS uses 30 × (age + 1)). Nonfunctional bladders may need cycling to judge true capacity.

q: Which statement about SWL in children is FALSE?
o: Renal SWL may be linked to hypertension
It suits stones after bladder reconstruction
e: After urinary reconstruction stone-free rates with SWL are only 12.5%; ureteroscopy or PCNL is better. SWL failure: large stone burden, long infundibulum, infundibulopelvic angle >45°, density >1000 HU. Renal SWL has been associated with later hypertension. URS and SWL are recommended for ureteral stones and renal stones <20 mm.

q: Under CDC criteria, whose tuberculin skin test (TST) is NOT positive?
o: A recent immigrant from India with 12 mm
A recent TB contact with 7 mm
A healthy US-born teacher with 11 mm
e: ≥5 mm: HIV, recent contacts, fibrotic chest x-ray, immunosuppression. ≥10 mm: recent immigrants from high-burden countries (BCG-vaccinated people usually fall here), drug injectors, high-risk settings. ≥15 mm: no risk factors. Local jurisdictions may set other cut-offs.

q: Which is NOT a risk factor for bladder stones in spinal cord injury?
e: Risk factors: complete lesion, Klebsiella UTI, Caucasian race, and indwelling catheters (CIC lowers stone incidence compared with indwelling catheters). Stones in otherwise normal people are rare; they form by heterogeneous (not homogeneous) nucleation around foreign bodies, infection or stasis with supersaturation; spinal cord injury patients are especially prone.

q: Which statement about the ureter in the female pelvis is FALSE?
o: It passes beneath the uterine artery
It runs posterior to the ovary first
It lies medial to the uterosacral
It tunnels through the cardinal ligament
e: The ureter runs posterior to the ovary, then medially under the broad ligament base, beneath the uterine artery (it turns anteriorly into the cardinal ligament tunnel), close to the cervix; it lies lateral to the anterior part of the uterosacral ligament (which arises at the greater sciatic foramen). It crosses under the ovarian vessels at the infundibulopelvic ligament: all sites of injury at radical hysterectomy.

q: Which statement about urethral tumour risk and neobladder is FALSE?
o: Prostatic stromal invasion predicts male urethral recurrence
A negative frozen urethral margin permits it despite CIS
Anterior vaginal wall induration bars a female neobladder
Preoperative prostatic urethral biopsy is mandatory
e: In men, prostatic stromal invasion is the main risk for urethral recurrence; in women, bladder neck or anterior vaginal wall involvement (bimanual examination under anaesthesia). Female neobladder became possible once skip lesions were shown rare without bladder neck tumour, and women stayed continent without a bladder neck. Intraoperative frozen section of the urethral margin is accurate; preoperative prostatic urethra/bladder neck biopsy is not mandatory. CIS, multifocality or extravesical disease do not preclude it if the margin is negative. Urethral recurrence: ~10% of men, rare in women; follow with examination and urethral cytology.

q: Which statement about imaging for recurrence after prostate cancer treatment is TRUE (per the book)?
o: mpMRI finds local recurrence at low PSA
CT is reliable at PSA levels below 10
TRUS beats DRE for radiorecurrent cancer
Bone scan is useful at PSA under 1 ng/mL
e: After RP, CT and bone scan add little below PSA 10 ng/mL; mpMRI sensitivity up to 86% at PSA 0.4–1.4 ng/mL. After radiotherapy, TRUS is no better than DRE and CT is irrelevant below PSA 20; contrast, spectroscopy and diffusion MRI improve detection. Update: PSMA PET/CT is now recommended (EAU, NCCN) for BCR and detects disease at much lower PSA than MRI or choline PET; the book's comparison is with older PET tracers.

q: Which statement about abdominal masses in infants is FALSE?
o: Wilms tumour is the commonest malignant one
Premature infants have weak abdominal walls
Renal causes make up about two-thirds
Mesoblastic nephroma is a solid neonatal mass
e: Neuroblastoma is the commonest malignant abdominal tumour in infants, then Wilms. Renal pathology accounts for about two-thirds of neonatal masses; solid ones include neuroblastoma, mesoblastic nephroma, teratoma and enlargement from renal vein thrombosis. The abdominal wall is weak in premature babies and sometimes with hydronephrosis.

q: Which statement about ureters during reconstruction is FALSE?
o: A taenial flap valve suits colon, not ileum
Ileum allows the easiest antireflux implant
Secondary VUR often resolves after augmentation
For TUU the recipient ureter is not mobilised
e: Nonrefluxing implants are easiest into colon (taenial tunnel, as in ureterosigmoidostomy) or stomach; ileum is hardest (Griffith split nipple, LeDuc trough, Abol-Enein serosal tunnel, reinforced nipples). Most secondary reflux resolves after successful reconstruction. Transureteroureterostomy: reimplant the better ureter; mobilise only the crossing ureter with its adventitia, keep it tension free and avoid angulation under the IMA. Bowel preparation is given even if bowel is not planned.

q: Which statement about paediatric ureteroscopy is FALSE?
o: It is done under general anaesthesia
Irrigant should be isotonic and warm
Ureteral injury is its commonest complication
e: Complications: mucosal flaps, perforation, false passage, avulsion; ureteral injury is commonest. Isotonic, body-temperature irrigant avoids hypothermia and hyponatraemia. Done under GA. Contraindicated with stone burden >20 mm or anatomy preventing retrograde access. Distal ureteral stones are best managed ureteroscopically. Perioperative antibiotics for instrumentation. Stent after the procedure for solitary kidney, staghorn, large ureteral stone, prior obstruction or abnormal anatomy, or to dilate a narrow ureter.

q: Which statement about genitourinary TB is FALSE?
o: Sterile pyuria is a typical finding
About 80% of GU TB involves the kidney
Ascending spread is the main route
e: Haematogenous spread is by far the commonest route, confined to the GU tract or disseminated. 80% involves the kidney; sterile pyuria or haematuria are typical; symptoms nonspecific with <20% constitutional. Untreated: fibrosis, renal failure, infertility. Chronic prostatitis resistant to antibiotics may be TB.

q: Which statement about bladder stone treatment is FALSE?
o: SWL suits patients with an AUS or prosthesis
Haematuria with LUTS is the usual presentation
e: Chemodissolution alone is slow and incomplete, now an adjunct; it is effective for (and prevents) encrustation of long-term catheters. SWL is an option with an artificial sphincter or penile prosthesis (avoid endoscopic damage), neobladder stones and high-risk patients. Percutaneous approaches are safe, effective and spare the urethra. Options: medical, SWL, transurethral lithotripsy, suprapubic cystolithotomy or cystolithotripsy, open surgery. Commonest presentation: haematuria with LUTS.

q: During transvaginal incontinence surgery, the nerves to the urethra are best protected by knowing they run:
o: In the midline beneath the urethra
Far laterally in the vaginal wall
Through the obturator canal to the bladder neck
Within the arcus tendineus fascia pelvis
e: Somatic and autonomic nerves travel on the lateral vaginal walls; incise the anterior wall away from them to prevent type III (ISD) incontinence. The female bladder neck has inner longitudinal fibres continuing to the meatus, a weak circular layer and little adrenergic innervation.

q: Which statement about neobladder construction is FALSE?
o: Use the old anastomosis site after bowel resection
The pouch should be fully detubularised
e: Antireflux mechanisms do not appear necessary to protect the upper tracts or prevent infection (intermediate term). Detubularise completely and reconfigure into a sphere for a low-pressure reservoir of 300–500 mL; ileum or ileum plus colon have the best properties; preserve the blood supply. After prior bowel resection, take down the old anastomosis and use that segment. Metal staples are stone niduses (hemi-Kock experience; intracorporeal stapled pouches). Afferent nipple stenosis was a late hemi-Kock complication (nephrostomy, endoscopic incision).

q: The minimum salvage radiotherapy dose after radical prostatectomy recommended by ASTRO (1999) and AUA (2013) is:
e: Doses up to 76 Gy have been reported with reasonable toxicity; dose escalation was tested in SAKK 09/10. Salvage RT should be discussed with any man with nonmetastatic rising PSA after RP; consider ADT with it, especially for high-risk features (RTOG 9601 showed survival benefit with 2 years of bicalutamide). Update: RADICALS-RT, RAVES and GETUG-AFU 17 favour early salvage over routine adjuvant RT.

q: Spinal ultrasound to look for occult dysraphism is possible only:
o: At any age with a sacral dimple
e: After 6 months, ossified posterior elements block the acoustic window, so MRI is used. Atypical dimples (off-centre, >2.5 cm from the anal verge, or deeper than 0.5 cm) have a 40% rate of occult dysraphism; hair tufts are also markers. Myelomeningocele carries latex allergy risk.

q: Which statement about bladder outlet procedures in neurogenic children is FALSE?
o: Bulking agents are not very effective in children
An AUS allows prompt continence with voiding
Fascial slings work better in girls than boys
e: Young-Dees-Leadbetter has limited success in neurogenic sphincter incompetence (poor muscle tone). The artificial urinary sphincter is the only procedure giving prompt continence while preserving spontaneous voiding; place it at the bladder neck in girls and prepubertal boys; if CIC and augmentation are needed anyway, native-tissue procedures avoid erosion, infection and mechanical failure. Fascial slings: better in girls; success 40–100%. Bladder neck closure unmasks detrusor hostility (lower compliance, more overactivity): assess urodynamics. Bladder neck division with a continent stoma is the ultimate step, only for reliable catheterisers. Wrap procedures: >90% continence but difficult catheterisation, especially in boys.

q: A 9-year-old has a 4 mm distal ureteral stone, normal labs and controlled pain. Best initial management:
e: Stones <5 mm usually pass; tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily (low-grade evidence, off-label); if not passed in 4–6 weeks, ureteroscopy. Larger stones are more likely to need intervention.

q: Which statement about diagnosing GU TB is FALSE?
o: MRI is the routine first imaging test
Urine AFB culture is the gold standard
First-void urine is the best sample
Every patient needs a chest x-ray
e: Gold standard: positive acid-fast bacilli culture from urine (first void best) or tissue. Alternatives: nucleic acid amplification, granulomas on histology. Imaging varies by site; MRI is not superior enough to CT/IVU for routine use. Chest x-ray excludes infectious pulmonary TB. Ureteral strictures look pipestem or beaded; bladder contracture is late, commoner in developing countries.

q: Which statement about stones in augmented or diverted bladders is FALSE?
o: Mucus acts as a nidus and biofilm
e: Haematuria-dysuria syndrome follows stomach, not ileum. Ileum/colon cause hyperchloraemic acidosis and hypercalciuria. Recurrent infection with urease-splitters (Proteus, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella) is the main cause; mucus forms a nidus and biofilm. All treatment modalities can be used. Prevention: complete stone clearance, treat infection, correct anatomy, reduce mucus, absorbable sutures.

q: Which statement about pelvic floor anatomy is FALSE?
o: Levator ani is supplied by the S2 root
Coccygeus runs from the sacrospinous ligament
Pubovisceral muscle slings the pelvic organs
e: Levator ani (iliococcygeus, puborectalis, pubococcygeus; named by attachments) is supplied by S4 (book). Pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus arise from the tendinous arc of the levator ani; the pubovisceral part slings, inserts into or attaches to viscera. Coccygeus runs from the sacrospinous ligament to sacrum and coccyx, completing the diaphragm. The arcus tendineus fascia pelvis runs from the pubic bone to the ischial spine.

q: Which statement about preserving continence at cystectomy is FALSE?
o: Control the dorsal venous complex carefully
Dissect deep anterior to male urethra
e: Rhabdosphincter fibres and pudendal innervation are concentrated anterior and lateral to the proximal urethra in both sexes, so avoid deep bites and excess dissection anteriorly; control the DVC. In women, leave the endopelvic fascia and levators. Preserving neurovascular bundles may help continence (nonrandomised data).

q: Which is NOT a requirement for salvage radical prostatectomy?
o: Life expectancy of at least 10 years
e: Ideal candidates: ≥10 years' life expectancy, no metastases, biopsy-proven local recurrence and ideally PSA <10 ng/mL. Separate node sampling is not required (frozen section first is reasonable).

q: Which statement about the newborn foreskin is FALSE?
o: Adhesions should be separated at birth
e: The newborn foreskin is adherent; do not separate adhesions unless circumcising. Complications: infection, meatal stenosis (healing of the denuded glans or frenular artery injury), too much/too little skin, cicatrix, even death. Infants under 6 months and uncircumcised boys have more UTIs.

q: Which statement about bowel segments for augmentation is FALSE?
o: Ileum shows the least urodynamic abnormality
Removing the ileocaecal valve can cause diarrhoea
Stomach is first choice in normal children
Bowel should be detubularised and reconfigured
e: Stomach is reserved for short gut or heavy pelvic irradiation. Ileum has the lowest basal pressure and least motor activity; problem contractions occur in about 5% (6% needed re-augmentation). Detubularise and make a sphere to maximise volume, blunt contractions and improve compliance. Removing ileum plus ileocaecal valve can cause diarrhoea (10% of neurogenic patients); preserve the terminal 15–20 cm ileum (B12). Bowel obstruction ~3%. Gastric segments: early satiety; possible increased tumour risk.

q: Which cause of hypercalciuria in a child is usually accompanied by hypercalcaemia?
e: Bartter, Dent disease and dRTA have normal serum calcium; idiopathic hypercalciuria by definition does. Hypercalciuria and hypocitraturia are the commonest abnormalities and raise recurrence; low volume and high sodium are common; uric acid stones are <5% in children. Work-up: 24-h urine for volume, calcium, citrate, oxalate, uric acid, sodium, pH, creatinine.

q: Which statement about TB drug treatment is FALSE?
o: Ethambutol can cause red-green colour blindness
e: Ethambutol is rarely hepatotoxic; its toxicity is ocular. Streptomycin is not hepatotoxic but not US first line. Start isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (standard 2HRZE/4HR). MDR prevalence in the US was 1.2% (2012). Rifampicin resistance is a surrogate for MDR. Correction: MDR = resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin; the book's definition fits old XDR; WHO 2021 XDR = MDR/RR + fluoroquinolone + bedaquiline or linezolid. Book keys pyrazinamide as likely active in XDR.

q: Which statement about urethral, prostatic and preputial stones is FALSE?
o: Urethral stones are about 10% of stones
Prostatitis symptoms triple prostatic stone risk
e: Urethral calculi are 0.3–1% of stone disease; usual presentation is acute painful retention from impaction (complete obstruction is rare). One prostatitis symptom makes a significant prostatic calculus 3.2 times likelier. Preputial calculi: severe phimosis, poor hygiene, low socioeconomic status; plain films show them in 14%. (The book's outline then lists chapters 96–104 on renal tumours.)

q: During sacrospinous ligament fixation, the structure at greatest risk lying just behind the ligament is:
e: The sacral plexus (and pudendal nerve) lie immediately posterior to the sacrospinous ligament as they leave the greater sciatic foramen; the ischial spine and ligament are key landmarks for vault suspension.

q: Which statement about continence after orthotopic neobladder is FALSE?
e: Daytime continence develops over 3–6 months in 80–90% of both sexes; nocturnal continence lags (obligate nocturnal diuresis early), persistent in 20–50%, improving beyond 12 months with timed voiding; reassure, no anticholinergics or urodynamics. Continence depends on age, segment and prostate-sparing technique. Retention: 4–10% of men, 20–60% of women; all candidates must be willing to self-catheterise (10–40%). Late female retention is from posterior pouch displacement kinking the urethra; uterine preservation seems most promising. New leakage after good function: check post-void residual first.

q: Which is NOT a recognised side effect of androgen deprivation therapy?
e: ADT causes hot flushes, osteoporosis, loss of libido and ED, fatigue, anaemia, metabolic changes and depression, not mania. Men with a rising PSA should be risk-stratified (Gleason score, PSA doubling time, interval to recurrence; Pound 1999) and treated according to risk of local vs systemic relapse and competing mortality. Update: EAU defines low- and high-risk BCR; EMBARK (2023) showed benefit of enzalutamide in high-risk BCR.

q: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia has one palpable gonad. Which diagnosis is ruled out?
e: A palpable gonad excludes female CAH (ovaries are not palpable) and pure gonadal dysgenesis (streak gonads). Symmetric findings suggest global disorders (CAH, androgen insensitivity); nonpalpable gonads suggest CAH. Ambiguous genitalia must be evaluated before nursery discharge because salt-wasting CAH is an emergency.

q: Which statement about metabolic effects of cystoplasty is FALSE?
o: Ileal augments raise the serum chloride
e: Gastric mucosa secretes HCl and blocks chloride resorption: hypokalaemic hypochloraemic alkalosis after GI illness. Hyperchloraemic acidosis was first seen after ureterosigmoidostomy; virtually every ileal/colonic augment raises chloride and lowers bicarbonate, but significant acidosis is rare with normal renal function. Haematuria-dysuria after gastrocystoplasty affects almost all sensate patients (milder in neurogenic patients; less with antral segments; worse with incontinence or poor renal function).

q: Which is NOT used in the treatment of cystinuria?
e: Cystinuria: impaired reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine. Treatment: high fluids, alkalinisation to pH >7.0 (potassium citrate), thiols (D-penicillamine, α-mercaptopropionylglycine/tiopronin). Thiazides treat hypercalciuria. A 2-cm cystine renal stone: PCNL gives the best clearance (SWL is poor).

q: Which statement about Schistosoma haematobium is FALSE?
o: Worms live in perivesical venous plexus
Its egg has a terminal spine
e: The host is Bulinus (Biomphalaria: S. mansoni; Oncomelania: S. japonicum). Terminal spined eggs; adults (3–5 years) live in the perivesical plexus; cercariae penetrate skin and become schistosomules. Pathology is mainly immune reaction to eggs. About 112 million infected, 1 billion at risk. Katayama fever is the acute syndrome. Praziquantel is the only WHO-approved drug.

q: Which pairing of vaginal level and blood supply is FALSE?
o: Lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes
Labial fat pads: external pudendal vessels
e: Upper vagina: uterine arteries; middle and inferior: vaginal arteries; lowest part: internal pudendal artery, draining to sacral, common iliac and superficial inguinal nodes (upper parts to internal/external iliac). Labial fat pads: external pudendal branches of the femoral vessels. The round ligament leaves via the internal ring over the external iliac artery to end in the labia (male homologue: gubernaculum).

q: Which statement about neobladder complications is FALSE?
o: Small pouch stones need endoscopic removal
An undrained leak needs early open repair
e: Undrained leak: percutaneous drain first, then nephrostomies; avoid early open revision. ~25% have asymptomatic bacteriuria; after 6 months symptomatic infection is rare. Remove stones endoscopically while small. Local pelvic recurrence (<10%) rarely affects function; treat with systemic chemotherapy ± radiotherapy. Women with persistent incontinence: check for pouch-vaginal fistula (omental interposition helps prevent it). Most late complications are endoscopically manageable. Early morbidity/mortality equal ileal conduit. Node-positive at surgery: complete neobladder and give adjuvant chemotherapy (up to 30% long-term survival).

q: Which statement about infant hydroceles is FALSE?
o: A fluctuating hydrocele means a patent processus
e: A communicating (volume-changing) hydrocele means a patent processus vaginalis and hernia risk; repair a symptomatic hernia in the newborn period. A large scrotal hydrocele may still resorb (distinguish from abdominoscrotal hydrocele). Undescended testes: 30% of preterm and 3% of term neonates; unlikely to descend after 6 months.

q: Which statement about catheterisable channels is FALSE?
o: Nipple valves fail more than flap valves
Monti tubes use tapered small bowel
Stomal stenosis is the commonest problem
e: Continence with an appendix (Mitrofanoff) can be achieved with a 2-cm tunnel; keep the channel to skin short. Stomal stenosis is commonest (10–20%); incontinence is rare. Alternatives: ureter, fallopian tube, Monti/Yang tapered bowel. Nipple valves (Kock) fail in ≥15%, more than flap valves. Most patients prefer catheterising an abdominal stoma to the urethra. Before ureterosigmoidostomy, confirm anal continence (manometry, EMG, upright oatmeal enema). Autoaugmentation gives a modest volume increase, so adequate preoperative capacity matters. Ureterocystoplasty is effective but needs a megaureter draining a poor kidney.

q: Which drug is NOT associated with renal stones or nephrocalcinosis?
e: Topiramate and acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitors): hypocitraturia and calcium phosphate stones. Loop diuretics: hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis. Indinavir crystallises. Spinal deformity can displace the kidney, raising organ injury risk at PCNL; PCNL relative indications: >20 mm, lower pole >1 cm, adverse anatomy. Up to 50% of children with reconstructed bladders form stones (stasis, bacteria, mucus, foreign body).

q: Which statement about lymphatic filariasis is FALSE?
e: DEC can blind patients with onchocerciasis and cause encephalopathy with heavy Loa loa. Doxycycline kills Wolbachia, reducing microfilariae. W. bancrofti: 90%; causes chyluria, hydrocele, scrotal/penile lymphoedema; obstruction follows repeated reinfection; long-term residents (not visitors) are affected; most are asymptomatic. 99% of onchocerciasis is sub-Saharan.

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Pelvic organs are supplied by inferior hypogastric plexus
Perineal tears can damage the internal sphincter
The peritoneum is reached via posterior fornix
The gluteal arteries come from anterior division
e: Superior gluteal artery: posterior division of internal iliac (book answer). Peritoneal access through the posterior fornix (rectouterine pouch). Perineal body damage in labour can injure internal anal sphincter fibres. Inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus supplies pelvic organs. Transversalis fascia (outer stratum) is continuous with endopelvic and lateral pelvic fascia; endopelvic fascia extends from uterine artery to vagina–levator fusion. Trigonal squamous (vaginal) metaplasia is normal in premenopausal women. Imaging: translabial US for mesh, bulking agents, implants; MRI is most comprehensive without radiation; T2 MRI is best for urethral diverticula.

q: Which statement about neobladder outcomes is FALSE?
o: Silent stones and strictures need imaging
QoL studies prove neobladder is superior
e: QoL studies are underpowered and biased; no diversion is proven superior, though body image is better with neobladders; preoperative education is key. Long-term follow-up: renal ultrasound, chemistry and B12 every 1–2 years (silent strictures, stones, B12 deficiency). ERAS: no bowel prep, alvimopan; not continuous IV opioids. Robotic cystectomy with extracorporeal diversion: smaller incision, less blood loss, but no shorter stay or fewer complications (MSKCC RCT; RAZOR later showed non-inferior PFS). Conduit late problems: stomal stenosis, hernia, pyelonephritis, stones, obstruction, renal deterioration; continent cutaneous: efferent mechanism problems needing revision.

q: Which statement about urinalysis in children is FALSE?
o: Continuous wetting in a girl suggests ectopic ureter
A positive dipstick alone confirms haematuria
Hypercalciuria is the commonest found cause
e: A positive dipstick needs microscopy; no RBCs means haemoglobinuria or myoglobinuria. Hypercalciuria is the commonest identified cause of asymptomatic MH. Continuous leakage in a girl suggests ectopic ureter. Secondary incontinence occurs after >6 months dry. Children who retain stool nearly always retain urine (few hold only urine). VCUG is needed to diagnose posterior urethral valves.

q: Which statement about long-term augmentation risks is FALSE?
o: Tumours have appeared 4 years after cystoplasty
e: Bacteriuria is common with CIC; treat for fever, pain, incontinence, haematuria or urea-splitting organisms; routine irrigation clears mucus. Stones are mostly struvite, less after gastrocystoplasty. Earliest tumour 4 years after cystoplasty; yearly endoscopic surveillance eventually. Delayed perforation in ~5% (Indiana 32/330, mean 4.3 years), mostly neurogenic; sigmoid was the only significant risk; treat by immediate surgical repair. A third need further surgery. In pregnancy the pedicle is deflected laterally; UTI risk rises.

q: Which TB intervention should NOT be delayed 4–6 weeks after starting drugs?
o: Reimplant for a distal ureteric stricture
e: Delay lets inflammation settle, bacillary load fall and lesions stabilise. Indications: relieve obstruction, drain infection, remove nonfunctioning infected kidneys, treat resistant hypertension, reconstruct. Relapse up to 22%.

q: Which statement about Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is FALSE?
o: It predisposes to Wilms and hepatoblastoma
It is caused by a chromosome 3p mutation
e: Chromosome 11p15.5. Features: macroglossia, nephromegaly, organomegaly, macrosomia, hemihypertrophy, neonatal hypoglycaemia. Tumours: adrenal carcinoma, Wilms, hepatoblastoma, rhabdomyosarcoma. Prepubertal testicular/paratesticular tumours: teratoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, epidermoid cyst, yolk sac tumour, germ cell tumour. Only 11% of girls in an abuse clinic had suggestive physical findings, so normal examination does not exclude abuse.

q: Which statement about urinary schistosomiasis is FALSE?
o: Sandy patches are submucosal egg deposits
Urine egg microscopy is first line
Its bladder cancer is mostly urothelial
e: Bladder cancer is mostly squamous, often well differentiated or verrucous, with a fair prognosis. Polyps, sandy patches, calcified bladder outline, distal strictures with hydronephrosis. Urine egg counts are the first-line gold standard (PCR, serology not first line; biopsies for difficult cases). Renal autotransplant is not used for schistosomal ureteral lesions. Echinococcal renal cysts: spillage can cause anaphylaxis. (Book outline then lists chapters 61 and 62.)

q: Which statement about urethral calculi is FALSE?
o: Migratory stones are small and multiple
Primary urethral stones are mainly struvite
Most lodge in the posterior urethra
They are commoner in males, with two age peaks
e: Migratory stones are usually solitary and larger than primary ones; most are migratory, held up by stricture, meatal stenosis or BPH, and may come from the upper tract as well as the bladder; concomitant bladder and upper tract stones in 18% and 2%. Male predominance with peaks in early childhood and the 4th–5th decades. Posterior urethral stones up to 78%; onset is abrupt; anterior stones may be palpable. Primary stones form behind strictures or in diverticula with infection or foreign body: small, round, coreless, mostly struvite; organisms E. coli, Proteus, enterococci.

q: Which statement about diagnosing urethral calculi is FALSE?
o: Most are radiolucent on plain films
A penile linear probe can scan the urethra
e: Most urethral stones are radio-opaque. 78% present with acute painful retention, 22% with LUTS. Retrograde urethrography is the mainstay; TRUS shows prostatic urethral stones; a 10 MHz linear probe on the dorsal penis screens the urethra; look for coexisting upper tract stones.

q: Which statement about treating urethral calculi is FALSE?
o: Push anterior stones back to bladder
Ventral meatotomy can reduce urethral trauma
e: Anterior stones can rarely be pushed back and this should not be tried; milk out only small smooth ones; holmium laser is least traumatic; ventral meatotomy allows controlled removal. Posterior stones can be pushed back for SWL (~60% stone-free) or intracorporeal lithotripsy; laser is less traumatic with 85–90% success. Hair-bearing grafts regrow hair in 3–6% despite epilation.

q: Which statement about stone risk is FALSE?
o: Loss of gut flora can cause enteric hyperoxaluria
e: Long-term antibiotics deplete gut bacteria (including oxalate degraders), causing enteric hyperoxaluria and more stones. After transplantation, calcineurin inhibitors and steroids promote calculi.

q: In urinary undiversion, most complications and reoperations relate to:
e: Key: understand the original pathology; achieve an effective antireflux mechanism without obstruction. In a 26-year series of 216 patients, bladder management (augmentation as needed; Young-Dees-Leadbetter for poor outlet) was straightforward; 23 needed reoperation for reflux and 10 for obstruction.

q: Which cutaneous TB manifestation can present early in TB disease?
e: Tuberculids are hypersensitivity reactions to disseminated MTBC antigens; culture and usually PCR negative.

q: Compared with open surgery, robotic cystectomy with extracorporeal diversion has shown:
o: A shorter hospital stay in an RCT
e: Large series and the MSKCC RCT showed no reduction in stay or complications; oncologic outcomes appear similar (RAZOR 2018: non-inferior progression-free survival).

q: In a child with reconstructed bladder, up to what proportion develop bladder stones?
e: Stasis, bacterial colonisation, retained mucus and foreign bodies (staples, non-absorbable sutures) all contribute.
